title: Make Your Swords the Judges of Your Critics' Necks
intro: This poem is attributed to Antara ibn Shaddad. The popular printings of his diwan head it “on his raid against the Banu Hariqa”, and in the Sira of Antar, the folk epic of his life, he recites a version of it after routing that tribe and killing their champion al-Akhyal. It opens with maxims of pride (judge your critics with the sword, leave a house of humiliation, defy the coward who holds you back), then turns to Antara's own boast: counted among the slaves, he has proved his lineage with spear and sword, killed the enemy's best men and owns his black mother without shame; a brief turn to love ends in two lines that prefer death with honour to life with disgrace. It is not in his old diwan: Muhammad Sa'id Mawlawi's critical edition has it neither in the recensions of al-A'lam al-Shantamari and al-Batalyawsi nor among the pieces he gathered from other books; it is found instead in the printings that followed Iskandar Agha Abkarius's diwan (Beirut, 1864), which, Mawlawi notes, gathered what the folk epic has along with the old recension. Its maxims are still quoted under Antara's name: al-Hashimi printed most of it in his anthology Jawahir al-Adab, and Amin Sa'id's commentary marks its last two lines as maxims.

translation: Make your swords the judges of your critics' necks,
and if you stop at a house of humiliation, move on.
1.sharh: Answer those who blame you with the sword, not with words, and never stay where you are held cheap. The poem opens with maxims of pride that Antara then proves on himself.

translation: If you are tried by a wrongdoer, be a wrongdoer;
if you meet with insolent men, be insolent.
2.sharh: Meet wrong with wrong and insolence with insolence, since a man who is mild with the unjust only invites more. Amr ibn Kulthum says the same: “Let no one act rashly against us, or we will outdo the rashness of the rash.”

translation: If a coward forbids you, on a day of battle,
fearing for you in the crush of the army,
3.sharh: When a coward tries to hold you back from battle, saying he fears for you in the press of the armies, he is really asking you to share his fear. The sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: defy what he says and pay him no heed,
and charge in the front rank when the clash is due.
4.sharh: Ignore the coward's warning and take your place in the front rank when the fighting starts. The previous line is the condition, and this one the answer.

translation: Choose for yourself a place that lifts you high,
or die nobly in the shade of battle dust.
5.sharh: Seek a rank that raises you above others, and if you cannot reach it, die nobly in battle. Between greatness and an honourable death he allows no middle way.

translation: No fortress will save you from the blows of death,
though you build it of solid rock.
6.sharh: No stronghold, however well built, keeps death away, so fleeing battle gains a man nothing. The line recalls the Quran: “Wherever you are, death will overtake you, even in towers built high.”

translation: For a young man, death in honour is better
than a night spent captive to a kohl-dark eye.
7.sharh: A young man is better dead with his honour than living as love's prisoner, his nights given over to a beautiful woman's eyes. Love that keeps him from glory is another kind of slavery.

translation: If I am counted among the slaves, my ambition
rises above the Pleiades and the unarmed Simak.
8.sharh: Even if men count him a slave, his ambition reaches higher than the stars. Here the poem turns from general advice to Antara himself, born a slave because his mother was one.

translation: Or if the horsemen of Abs deny my lineage,
my spearhead and my sword acknowledge me.
9.sharh: If the knights of his own tribe deny that he is one of them, his spear and sword vouch for him. His father owned him as a son only after he proved himself in battle.

translation: With my lance and my Indian blade I won the heights,
not by kinship, nor by a host of kinsmen.
10.sharh: He won his standing with his own weapons, not through powerful relatives or a large clan behind him. Whatever glory he has, he made himself.

translation: I flung my colt into the dust of battle and it plunged in,
while fire struck from the edges of the blades.
11.sharh: He drove his young horse into the dust of battle, where the blades met so hard that sparks flew from their edges like fire from a flint.

translation: It plunged into the dust white-stockinged, and once
it had seen the fight, it came back stockinged no more.
12.sharh: The horse rode into battle with white legs and came back with them red, so stained with blood that the white could no longer be seen.

translation: I dealt the Banu Hariqa a calamity
when I speared al-Akhyal through the heart.
13.sharh: He struck the Banu Hariqa a heavy blow when he speared their champion al-Akhyal through the heart. In the Sira, al-Akhyal's death sends the tribe fleeing to the mountains, leaving their herds and families behind.

translation: I killed their horseman Rabi'a by force,
al-Haydhuban, and Jabir ibn Muhalhil,
14.sharh: He names the men he killed: their horseman Rabi'a, overcome by force, al-Haydhuban and Jabir ibn Muhalhil. Naming the dead turns a boast into a record of what he did.

translation: Rabi'a's two sons, al-Harish, and Malik,
and al-Zibriqan, who lay felled on the rocks.
15.sharh: The list of the dead goes on: the two sons of Rabi'a, al-Harish, Malik, and al-Zibriqan, left lying on the rocks. All of them are objects of “I killed” in the previous line.

translation: I am the son of a black-browed woman, like
a hyena grown up among the traces of a camp.
16.sharh: He declares without shame that he is the son of a black woman, and likens himself to a hyena reared among the ruins of abandoned camps: hardy, wild and bred in the desert.

translation: Her legs are like an ostrich's legs,
her hair is like peppercorns.
17.sharh: He describes his mother as those who taunt him would: legs as thin as an ostrich's, hair as tightly curled as peppercorns. What they mock as Abyssinian, he states plainly as his own.

translation: Her mouth beneath the veil is like
lightning flashing in the hanging dark.
18.sharh: Her teeth flash beneath her veil like lightning in the dark, and the darkness of her skin makes their whiteness brighter. The portrait the taunts began ends in praise.

translation: You who camp at al-Hima and its dwellings,
have you not seen me restless among the tents?
19.sharh: He turns to the beloved's people camped at al-Hima and asks whether they have not seen him wandering restlessly among their tents. The poem moves here from pride to love.

translation: Long has been your pride, and my abasement in love,
and strange it is: your pride, and my humbling.
20.sharh: They are proud and he is humbled by love, and the strange thing is that the man who refuses humiliation everywhere else accepts it from them. Love is the one master he obeys.

translation: Do not give me the water of life with humiliation;
give me instead, with honour, a cup of colocynth.
21.sharh: He would refuse even the water of life if it came with humiliation, and drink the bitterest colocynth if it came with honour. These closing lines are the poem's best-known maxims.

translation: The water of life with humiliation is like Hell,
and Hell with honour is the finest home.
22.sharh: A sweet life with humiliation is as bad as Hell, and Hell itself with honour is a better home. The poem ends as it began, with the refusal of disgrace.

2.2.5.head: اِجهَل
2.2.5.meaning: Be insolent: jahl here is rashness and aggression, the opposite of forbearance, not ignorance.

3.1.4-5.meaning: “A hateful day”: a day of battle.

4.1.5.meaning: Him, the coward. The editions have biha, “it”, his words.

4.2.1.head: أَقدِم
4.2.1.meaning: Charge, press forward: aqdim, said here without its hamza for the metre.

5.2.6.head: القَسطَل
5.2.6.meaning: Qastal: dust, the dust of battle.

7.2.5-6.head: طَرف أَكحَل
7.2.5-6.meaning: “A kohl-dark eye”: the dark-lidded eye of a beautiful woman.

8.2.3-4.head: السِّماك الأَعزَل
8.2.3-4.meaning: Al-Simak al-A'zal, “the unarmed Simak”: the star Spica, called unarmed because no star goes before it like a lance, as one goes before its twin, al-Simak al-Ramih.

9.1.4.head: عَبس
9.1.4.meaning: Abs: Antara's tribe, a branch of Ghatafan.

10.1.1.head: ذابِل
10.1.1.meaning: Dhabil: a lance, named for its slender, supple shaft.

10.1.2.head: مُهَنَّد
10.1.2.meaning: Muhannad: a sword of Indian steel.

12.1.3.head: مُحَجَّل
12.1.3.meaning: Muhajjal: a horse with white on its legs, “white-stockinged”.

13.1.3-4.head: بَنو حُرَيقَة
13.1.3-4.meaning: Banu Hariqa: a tribe in the Sira of Antar, which he raids and routs.

13.2.5.head: الأَخيَل
13.2.5.meaning: Al-Akhyal: in the Sira, al-Akhyal ibn Amr, champion of the Banu Hariqa, whom Antara spears through the chest. Some editors read it as “the proud one”.

15.1.3.head: الحَريش
15.1.3.meaning: Al-Harish, a man's name. Two printings have al-Haris.

15.2.1.head: الزِّبرِقان
15.2.1.meaning: Al-Zibriqan, a man's name; the word also means the moon.

16.1.5.meaning: Like him, the son. The editions have ka'annaha, “like her”, likening the mother to a hyena.

19.1.4.meaning: Al-Hima, “the protected land”: a reserved pasture; in poetry, often the beloved's country.

21.1.3-4.meaning: “The water of life”: the water life depends on, and the legendary spring of immortality.

21.2.5.head: الحَنظَل
21.2.5.meaning: Colocynth: a desert gourd proverbial for its bitterness.
